name: Ignatius of Antioch
knownFor: Bishop of Antioch whose seven letters, written under guard on the way to his death at Rome, warn the churches to keep to their bishops and to Christ who truly suffered.
dates: Died under the emperor Trajan, or later
place: Antioch in Syria; Smyrna and Troas on the road to Rome

keyWorks.title: Letter to the Romans
keyWorks.about: his plea that the church at Rome not save him from the beasts

keyWorks.title: Letter to the Smyrnaeans
keyWorks.about: against those who said Christ only seemed to suffer; where the phrase "Catholic Church" first appears, Cleveland Coxe says

keyWorks.title: Letter to Polycarp
keyWorks.about: to the bishop of Smyrna, asking him to care for the church at Antioch

traces: He told the churches to do nothing without their bishop, and wrote that "wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church." Cleveland Coxe, who edited the American edition of the letters, notes that this is the first use of that phrase in the early church's writings.
remembered: Polycarp of Smyrna, in his letter to the Philippians, holds up "the blessed Ignatius" as an example of patience.
Irenaeus of Lyon quotes the wheat line as the words of a man of the church condemned to the beasts. Eusebius of Caesarea gives Irenaeus's words as "As one of our people said."
Eusebius of Caesarea says his fame "is still celebrated by a great many."

uncertain: Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea, says almost all we know of him comes from his own letters. Eusebius adds that he was the second bishop of Antioch after Peter, and that report said he died by the beasts at Rome.

Which letters are his was argued for a long time. Fifteen carry his name; eight are set aside as forgeries. Daillé, in 1666, rejected all of them. Bishop Pearson defended the seven shorter Greek letters in 1672. William Cureton, in 1845, argued that only the three letters in a Syriac version were genuine; Bunsen agreed with him and Hefele did not. McGiffert wrote in 1890 that Zahn and Lightfoot had finally settled it for the shorter Greek letters, though he notes that some still denied them.
Eusebius's Chronicle dates his death to the tenth year of Trajan, about 107. Zahn and Lightfoot would say only that it was under Trajan. Harnack placed it under Hadrian.
Accounts of his martyrdom were written from the fourth century on. McGiffert says they contradict one another and cannot be relied on.
